verdict: OK to lend in Chikkamagaluru coffee curing and export, but only to curers with firm export orders and hedged receivables; avoid pure price-speculators holding green coffee inventory.
title: Chikkamagaluru Coffee Curing & Export: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**A curer buys green coffee from estate growers, cures it (drying, hulling, grading, sorting), and sells to exporters or roasters; cash comes back only after the shipment lands and the buyer pays.** India exports 75% of its coffee, 45% goes to the EU and Italy alone takes 16% [1]. So when a proposal lands, check the buyer list and the destination mix first; if one buyer or one country dominates, ask for the order book and past shipment documents.

## Where value and cash sit
**Value sits in grading quality and buyer relationships, not in the drying yard; cash sits in inventory and export receivables.** Peer CCL Products shows the pattern: Q2 FY27 turnover Rs 1,215.99 crore, up 7.8%, with double-digit volume growth but lower realisations because green coffee prices fell [5]. Gross margin still expanded 339 bps to 37.9% [4][6]. So when a proposal lands, check whether growth is volume-led or price-led; if the borrower's turnover rose only because prices rose, ask for volume and realisation separately.

## What has changed now
**Green coffee prices have fallen, so realisations are softer even where volumes are fine** [4][5][7]. The Coffee Board has launched the 'Indica Coffee' brand targeting Italy and the UK [1], and a Chikkamagaluru technical fair drew 80-plus companies in September 2026 [2]. Local sources say growers face labour shortage, weather variation and yield decline [2], and tea is spreading alongside coffee [3]. Note the local coverage is thin on curing-unit finances; lean on first principles and the CCL peer.

## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
**Pursue curers with confirmed export orders, EU/UK buyer relationships and a domestic instant-coffee fallback; avoid traders who hold green coffee hoping for a price rebound.** Take monthly stock statements, ageing of export receivables and buyer-wise shipment data. Structure against documents-against-payment receivables, since holding period is largely shipment transit time [9]. Cap exposure where more than 80% of export revenue comes from the top two destinations, as seen in peer SNCPL [10].

## Early-warning signs
**Watch inventory days rising while shipments fall, and receivables ageing past transit time.** If a borrower's stock grows but dispatch documents do not, ask for the godown register and buyer confirmations. If the top-buyer share crosses the peer benchmark [10], ask for a diversification plan. Currency exposure on export receivables needs a stated hedge policy [11].
watch: Inventory days rise while dispatches fall -> ask for godown register and buyer confirmations
Receivables age past shipment transit time -> seek DP/LC confirmation and reduce limit
Top two destinations exceed 80% of export revenue -> ask for diversification plan before enhancement
Turnover growth purely price-led -> reprice limit to volume-based assessment
Unhedged export receivables rise -> require hedge cover before next disbursement
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
news_why: Falling green coffee prices cut realisations; peer CCL missed revenue and PAT estimates.
